\begin{definition}[Binary encodings of prime numbers]
\lean{Randomized.PRIMESBin}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p045-b007,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p045-b008,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p046-b002
}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p004-b001}
\label{Randomized.PRIMESBin}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Randomized.PRIMES}
The language consists of exactly those Boolean strings whose binary value is a prime
number.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Composite-number verifier]
\lean{Randomized.compositeVerifier}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p004-b002}
\label{Randomized.compositeVerifier}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Randomized.eulerLiarRounds}
Given Boolean strings $x$ and $r$, return true if the binary value of $x$ is less than
$2$, return false if it equals $2$, and return true if it is even. In every other case,
return the negation of the result of the specified number of Euler-liar rounds on the
binary value of $x$, using $|x|+3$ rounds with parameter $2$ and randomness $r$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Euler liar round predicate]
\lean{Randomized.liarRound}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p004-b002}
\label{Randomized.liarRound}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.add, Complexity.BinArith.beq, Complexity.BinArith.gcd, Complexity.BinArith.jacobiModAlg, Complexity.BinArith.mod, Complexity.BinArith.powMod, Complexity.BinArith.sub, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.pairEncode}
Given a Boolean string $z$, decode it as a pair of Boolean strings and let $N$ be the
binary value of the first component. Form the encoded arithmetic quantities specified by
subtracting the encoding of $(N,[\mathrm{true}])$ from the first component, reducing the
binary value of the second component modulo that difference, adding the encoding of
$([\mathrm{true}],\cdot)$ to obtain $A$, and then test both that the encoded greatest
common divisor of $A$ and $N$ equals one and that the encoded Jacobi-symbol computation
for $(A,N)$ equals the encoded modular power with base $A$ and exponent given by the
tail of the difference, modulo $N$; return true exactly when both tests pass.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Liar-Round Test]
\lean{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_liarRound}
\label{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_liarRound}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.add, Complexity.BinArith.mod, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_add, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_beq, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_gcd, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_jacobiModAlg, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mod, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_powMod, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_sub, Complexity.BinArith.sub, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_and, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_tail, Randomized.liarRound, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{4}
For every bit string $z$, the function sending $z$ to the singleton list containing the
Boolean result of the liar-round test on $z$ is computable by a deterministic
finite-state Turing machine in time $C(n+1)^c$ on every input of length $n$, for some
natural numbers $C$ and $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Euler Liar Round Correctness]
\lean{Randomized.liarRound_pairEncode}
\label{Randomized.liarRound_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.add, Complexity.BinArith.beq, Complexity.BinArith.bitsVal_drop_one, Complexity.BinArith.gcd_pairEncode, Complexity.BinArith.jacobiModAlg_pairEncode, Complexity.BinArith.mod, Complexity.BinArith.powMod, Complexity.BinArith.sub, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal_bits, Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode, Randomized.IsEulerLiar, Randomized.eulerSample, Randomized.isEulerLiar_iff_emod, Randomized.liarRound, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $N$ be a natural number with $1<N$ and $N$ odd, and let $w$ be a finite bit string.
Encode $N$ by its binary expansion and pair it with $w$. The liar-round test on this
encoding returns true if and only if $A=1+\operatorname{bitsVal}(w)\bmod(N-1)$ is
coprime to $N$ and the Jacobi symbol of $A$ modulo $N$, regarded as an element of
$\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, equals $A^{(N-1)/2}$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Two-round composite test]
\lean{Randomized.compositeTest}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p046-b002}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p004-b002}
\label{Randomized.compositeTest}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.beq, Complexity.BinArith.lt, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.dropPrefixByLen, Randomized.liarRound, Randomized.takePrefixByLen, Turing.pairEncode}
Given a Boolean string $z$, decode its first component and let $N$ be the binary
expansion of its binary value; append three true bits to that first component to form
$u$. Return true if the encoded comparison says $N<2$, return false if it says $N=2$,
and return true if the first bit of the decoded first component is false. Otherwise,
split the second component using the encoded prefix length determined by the pair
$(u,\cdot)$, pair-encode each of the resulting two strings with $N$, and return the
negation of the conjunction of the two liar-round predicates on those encodings.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Composite Test]
\lean{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_compositeTest}
\label{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_compositeTest}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_beq, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_lt, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_normBits, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.append, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_and, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_headD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_ite, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_not, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Randomized.compositeTest, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_dropPrefixByLen, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_liarRound, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_takePrefixByLen}
\difficulty{4}
For every bit string $z$, form the integer represented by the first component of its
decoded pair. Define a Boolean test that returns true when this integer is less than
$2$, false when it equals $2$, true when its least significant bit is $0$, and otherwise
returns the negation of the conjunction of two liar-round tests, using respectively the
length-sized prefix and the next length-sized block of the second component after
appending three $1$ bits to the first component. The function sending $z$ to the
singleton list containing this test result is computable by a deterministic finite-state
Turing machine in time $C(n+1)^c$ on every input of length $n$, for some natural numbers
$C$ and $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composite test on encoded inputs]
\lean{Randomized.compositeTest_pairEncode}
\label{Randomized.compositeTest_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.beq, Complexity.BinArith.bitsVal_mod_two, Complexity.BinArith.lt, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal_bits, Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode, Randomized.compositeTest, Randomized.compositeVerifier, Randomized.dropPrefixByLen, Randomized.eulerLiarRounds, Randomized.liarRound_pairEncode, Randomized.takePrefixByLen, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
For any Boolean strings $x$ and $r$, the composite test applied to the encoding of
$(x,r)$ equals the composite verifier applied to $x$ and $r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Efficiency of the composite verifier]
\lean{Randomized.eff_compositeVerifier}
\label{Randomized.eff_compositeVerifier}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.boolVerifier, Randomized.compositeTest_pairEncode, Randomized.compositeVerifier, Randomized.eff_boolVerifier_of_test, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_compositeTest, Randomized.polyTimeModel}
\difficulty{1}
For Boolean strings $x$ and $r$, interpret each string as a nonnegative integer by
reading its bits in the order in which they occur, with the first bit having weight $1$.
The composite verifier accepts automatically when the integer represented by $x$ is less
than $2$, rejects when it equals $2$, and accepts when it is even. Otherwise it rejects
exactly when two successive Euler-liar rounds, each using $|x|+3$ bits of $r$ per round,
both identify the sampled value as an Euler liar for the integer represented by $x$.
This verifier, viewed as returning its Boolean decision as an optional Boolean value, is
efficient in the polynomial-time verifier model.
\end{theorem}

least significant, is a prime number belongs to BPP.

  {pdf-26d95080dbde-p007-b002}
Every binary string whose little-endian binary value is prime belongs to the class of
languages decidable by a finite randomized Turing machine in polynomial time with
acceptance probability at least $2/3$ on every input and halting on every choice
sequence of the prescribed length.
\end{theorem}
